articles.title: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis Could Be Great, But There's Some Things We Can't Ignore...
articles.summary: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis shows massive potential, but controversial changes like skill trees and modern hand-holding threaten to frustrate fans. And some of that food looks very suspicious.
body: The first thing that strikes you upon seeing the new Tomb Raider live-demoed on a massive 115” TV mere inches from your face, I can attest, is its visual fidelity: Legacy of Atlantis is absurdly pretty. Crammed with fine detail enough that every particle of dust and bat guano flitting through the stale air poses danger to your airways, it almost feels like it’s supposed to be funny when compared to the chunky textures and pointy polygons of the 32-bit original.

The game’s director Raul Siqueira puts it nicely during our session: “the secret to a good remake is knowing what to change, and what to leave well alone”. Absolutely. Preserving the essence of a thing is much more vital than slavishly recreating the original work, and this is certainly something that Legacy of Atlantis understands, aesthetically at least. It is unmistakably a modern interpretation of Lara Croft’s seminal adventure, an essential piece of gaming history arguably as important as Super Mario Bros. or Chuckie Egg (ask your dad).
points: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis shows massive potential, but controversial changes like skill trees and modern hand-holding threaten to frustrate fans.

articles.title: Before HBO’s The Last Of Us, An Entirely Different Adaptation Was Proposed
articles.summary: Naughty Dog's first effort to adapt The Last of Us for the screen was not as an HBO TV show, but a movie, a fact that recently began doing the rounds again on social media.
body: While not everyone agrees with the creative departures from the source material for the TV series on HBO, it's undeniably a success and one of HBO's biggest hits lately. Let's look back at how The Last of Us originated as a movie and run through the key developments that led to it becoming a TV show.
People across X recently discovered a post from Sony Pictures in 2014 declaring that The Last of Us was "soon to be a major motion picture."

This was a real, studio-sponsored image, not a fan mock-up. There was officially produced key art, showing Ellie wielding a knife. There was a "secret panel" at San Diego Comic-Con that year featuring director Sam Raimi, who was originally attached to produce the movie, having already had huge success at Sony with his Spider-Man films.
That The Last of Us was originally going to be a movie is not surprising given how many video game movies came before it and how many have been released since (with varying degrees of success).

articles.title: Brandon Sanderson’s Latest Sci-Fi Book has a Surprise Cosmere Connection
articles.summary: The immortal trickster and storyteller Hoid has appeared in so many of Sanderson’s books that some fans have accused the author of having a self-insert character. He even narrates his own series, Hoid’s Travails, which includes Tress of the Emerald Sea, Yume and the Nightmare Painter, and the…
body: Most of Brandon Sanderson’s fantasy books are set in the Cosmere, a galaxy where each planet has its own complex magic system connected by a common divine origin. Sanderson’s Cytoverse sci-fi series takes place in a different reality where Earth has vanished and the last remnants of humanity live on isolated planets, but the two worlds cross over for the first time in Blightfall, the latest Cytoverse book co-written by Sanderson and Janci Patterson.
You might assume this was part of some long-simmering plan from Sanderson to fuse the two universes, but Patterson tells Polygon that it happened completely on a whim.

“There was a thread on the 17th Shard fan forums where everybody was talking about the book and somebody made a joke that we should name a slug Hoid,” the writer says. “I didn’t know if it would pan out, but then I put it in the book and [Sanderson] didn’t stop me.”

articles.title: BioWare doesn't need advice for Mass Effect 4, says veteran designer, as long as "people get out of the way"
articles.summary: Original Mass Effect cinematic designer and Mass Effect 2 lead cinematic designer Armando Troisi has insisted the current BioWare team doesn't need outside advice on developing the next installment because so many of the people who built the original trilogy are still at the studio.
body: Asked what guidance they'd offer developers working on the new game, Troisi didn't think they had anything to add.

"It's hard for me to say because a lot of people that are on that project were there [during the originals]," Troisi told FRVR. "They know. Preston [Watamaniuk] is there, and Derek [Watts] is there, and Parish [Ley] is there, and they're the OGs, you know? I don't think there's anything that I could tell them that they don't know what to do."
Troisi left the studio after Mass Effect 2, but has confident in the team that remains behind.

"When I was leaving, everybody wrote on a card… he [Preston] said, 'passion and craft is excellence'… I think they've got both of those so I don't think that I can give them any more advice than they already have. They know this stuff," Troisi said.

articles.title: 40 Years Ago, Konami Changed the Video Game Industry Forever
articles.summary: New video games released in recent years might sell well, but they rarely transform the industry as a whole. We’ve played too many games across too many genres to believe there’s much left to explore that’s genuinely new.
body: First released in Japan on the Famicom Disk System as Akumajou Dracula on Sept. 26, 1986, Castlevania is a 2D platformer that kicked off a beloved series of games chronicling the adventures of the Belmont clan as they battle Dracula. To face that powerful nemesis, players must first vanquish a variety of creatures drawn from horror mythology, while navigating a treacherous castle filled with pits, staircases, gears, and dubious chicken feasts.

Back in 2018, Polygon ranked the best Castlevania games of all time. The sprawling list included more than 30 titles. Selections included portable triumphs (and disasters), a puzzle game, arcade releases, a fighting game, and plenty of platformers in 2D and 3D. The franchise has evolved a lot over the years, taking some surprising detours along the way with varying degrees of success. But all of that began with Simon Belmont’s journey into a castle in search of Count Dracula.
points: New video games released in recent years might sell well, but they rarely transform the industry as a whole.
We’ve played too many games across too many genres to believe there’s much left to explore that’s genuinely new.

articles.title: Gen-AI controversy aside, Crazy Taxi: World Tour feels like classic arcade Sega - and it's an absolute blast
articles.summary: Crazy Taxi was not my favourite Dreamcast game (please don't ask me to choose between the triumphant rhythm triptych of Rez, Space Channel 5, and Samba de Amigo, however), but there's a specific bit of it that's forever seared into my brain: the giddy thrill of cresting over that one…
body: As a moment, it's the kind of perfect melding of style and blissful arcade purity that seemed to define so much of Sega's Dreamcast-era output. And my recent half-hour hands-on with the upcoming Crazy Taxi: World Tour at Gamescom suggests the original's 90s skate-punk spirit and taut arcade thrills are - if perhaps not equal - alive and well in this, Sega's long-awaited revival.

Crazy Taxi poster boy Axel is back (hair still green, shirt still Hawaiian, attitude less abrasive, and six pack now demurely hidden), as is the music of The Offspring and Bad Religion. Meaning that in terms of pure vibes, World Tour feels a lot like 1999 never left.

articles.title: Samara Weaving's Gritty Action Sleeper Hit Officially Finds a New Home on Streaming
articles.summary: Samara Weaving is the perfect casting for Emma Frost, adding intense anticipation for Marvel’s X-Men reboot. Weaving has already established a knack for playing memorable female leads, thanks to her reputation as a talented scream queen.
body: The actor has appeared in thriller movies like Mayhem (2017), The Babysitter (2017), and Scream VI (2023) over the years, while also being a part of thrillers like Over Your Dead Body (2026). But one role in particular makes the best argument that she's the right fit to play the MCU's new White Queen.

Weaving belts out a memorable performance in both Ready or Not (2019) and its recent sequel, Ready or Not 2: Here I Come. The 2019 film, which showcases Weaving’s knack for horror and comedy, is now streaming on Netflix. This is the perfect time to watch this subversive gem while you wait for Weaving’s Frost in the upcoming X-Men movie.

Ready or Not opens with a strange ritual, where a man in a groom’s suit is hunted by his in-laws. The Le Domas family appears wearing ceremonial masks, pushing the event towards a grisly end. Fast-forward 20 years and we meet Alex Le Domas (Mark O'Brien), who is about to get married to Grace (Weaving).

articles.title: Ridley Scott's 158-Minute War Action Epic Is Officially a Global Streaming Sensation
articles.summary: Director Ridley Scott is not known for making small-scale films. His sci-fi films, like Blade Runner and the Alien franchise, remain staples within the genre, along with being some of his most well-known works.
body: Not all epics are made equal, however, and one particular epic didn't see much success until was released on streaming platforms in 2024.

2023's Napoleon can be best described as a sprawling epic of pageantry. When first released in theaters, it was largely considered a box office disappointment. Though it fared slightly better overseas, in the United States and Canada it grossed merely $61.5 million. With a gross of $160.9 million in other territories, it still fell short with a total gross of $222.4 million.

Napoleon seemed destined to fade away and be forgotten once its theatrical window closed. But as streaming tends to do with new audiences, things are not looking quite as hopeless for the future of this film.

articles.title: Left 4 Dead 2 writer says Valve intentionally 'leaked' its cinematic trailer to get around ESRB rules: 'I think we can't get trouble for that now'
articles.summary: It's strange to think about in hindsight, but Left 4 Dead 2 was a controversial game in the run-up to its release in November 2009—just one year after the original Left 4 Dead laid the foundations for today's enormous cooperative gaming scene.
body: Ultimately, Left 4 Dead 2 would prove a worthy follow-up to Valve's cooperative blaster. But it turns out there was some skulduggery afoot behind the scenes on Left 4 Dead 2, just not the kind that fans suspected. Shortly before the sequel's launch, a cinematic trailer—which would ultimately serve as Left 4 Dead 2's introductory cutscene—leaked onto the Internet. Now, it's been revealed that this 'leak' was orchestrated by Valve to evade the censorious watch of the Entertainment Software Ratings Board.

This is according to former Valve writer and Left 4 Dead designer Chet Faliszek, who revealed Valve's deliberate leak in a YouTube video about cut Left 4 Dead voice lines (via Ars Technica ). In the video, Faliszek explains why Left 4 Dead 2 had a large number of voice lines cut from the final game. One reason was that, at the time, Valve had run-ins with numerous countries and ratings boards over the series' depictions of violence and use of profane language.

articles.title: 'No One Puts Double Fine Out of Business Except for Me' — Tim Schafer Explains How He Kept Double Fine Afloat After Leaving Xbox
articles.summary: Tim Schafer, game designer and founder of Psychonauts developer Double Fine, gave a strong response after Xbox divested the studio as part of its massive restructuring efforts this summer.
body: Speaking with Bloomberg's Jason Schreier in a September 2026 interview, Schafer admitted that he knew something was up before Xbox’s divestment was officially announced — but he wasn’t about to go down without a fight.

"You’re like, 'Wait a second, we’re not going out like this,'" Schafer explained. "Some people said, 'I’m checking out, this is one too many battles for me.’ But for the rest of us, it’s like a creative awakening."

"No one puts Double Fine out of business except for me," he continued. "Asha’s not going to shoot my dog. I’m going to shoot it. But I’m not going to shoot it, because it’s going to do great. A lot of people want to walk the dog."

Thankfully, Double Fine was able to retain its intellectual property and become fully independent, though it did have to lay off a quarter of its staff as a result of this change. That isn’t stopping it from making more games, though, as the developer recently published a Kickstarter for its next project — with the addendum that if it raises $100 million, they’ll also make Brutal Legend 2.

articles.title: Wonder Woman Casting Rumors Heat Up as Fans Suspect James Gunn Secretly Picked Adria Arjona for the Role
articles.summary: DC fans are convinced the DCU's Wonder Woman will be played by Adria Arjona after she posted a video of her workout routine ahead of Man of Tomorrow.
body: As the DCU navigates its ups and downs, all eyes are on DC Studios co-CEO and director James Gunn to deliver next year's Superman sequel. Arjona is just one part of the equation that will help bring David Corenswet's Last Son of Krypton back to the big screen, but fans think she knows more than she's letting on when it comes to the part she'll play in the wider DCU.

Mixed in with a variety of other superhero parts – including Milly Alcock's Supergirl, Aaron Pierre's John Stewart, and Xolo Maridueña as Blue Beetle – Arjona was previously said to be playing the role of DC deep cut Maxima. She reportedly landed the part in April of this year, but fans think Gunn and company are misleading fans in hopes of a big Sadie Sink/Spider-Man-style surprise with Man of Tomorrow.

articles.summary: This is the first Saturday in a month I've woken up without a blocked nose or a mucus-hurling cough. Trips to Spain, Sweden, and Germany in quick succession and loaded on top of a cross country bike ride may have been a touch to much for my ageing body. Still, at last, I am well.
body: Still, at last, I am well. In body, if not in spirit. So, better start playing some games then, right?

Edwin I've managed to persuade the Gamer Network overlords to loan me a gaming laptop for reviews, so I'll be trying out various swankier 3D things on that, including Blood of Dawnwalker. I also need to finish Pathologic 3. I'm open to suggestions for recent, higher-end fare. Are they still making those Silent Hill games? What about Jak & Daxter?

articles.title: gamescom Apologizes for Its Initial Response to Thefts, Promises Improved Security Measures
articles.summary: gamescom has provided a second response regarding the theft of developers’ equipment during its event, offering an apology for its initial reaction to the ordeal.
body: On August 28, 2026, indie developer Ryan Laley uploaded a video to X/Twitter claiming that all of his laptops had been stolen at gamescom. He wasn’t the only one affected; several other developers spoke out with similar stories, saying their equipment had also been pilfered at the event.
gamescom responded to the ordeal on August 29, writing that while it was "very sad" about the situation, it "would like to inform [attendees] about general security regulations."

"Individual stand security can be booked separately, and exhibitors are advised to insure equipment against theft. This is noted in the terms and conditions of participation and the technical guidelines," it said. "...At an event of this size, however, there will always be individuals attempting to take advantage of the situation. Our security measures are designed to minimize such risks as effectively as possible.”

This statement didn’t go over well. A swath of fellow exhibitors, attendees, and onlookers online felt that gamescom’s reply placed blame on victims of the theft, slamming the event for its "unacceptable response."
points: gamescom has provided a second response regarding the theft of developers’ equipment during its event, offering an apology for its initial reaction to the ordeal.

articles.title: Game Director Finally Addresses His Rumored Foot Fetish–Wait, Not Kojima, The Other One
articles.summary: A prolific Japanese game developer has finally addressed all that weird foot imagery in his video games. What? No, I'm not talking about Hideo Kojima (he's busy hanging out with The Backrooms director right now, anyway).
body: “It's not necessarily something I’m consistently aware of--maybe it’s something subconscious coming through,” Miyazaki told The Guardian in response to a question about all the hand imagery in his upcoming action-RPG, The Duskbloods. "Take a look online and there’s a rumor that I have a bit of a thing for feet, but I’m not honestly sure where this comes from."

Though Miyazaki says he's not sure where the idea that he has a "thing for feet" comes from, it's something fans of his games have noticed for years. Whether we're talking The Maiden in Black from Demons' Souls or Priscilla (or Gwunevere, or Sister Friede, or Maneater Mildred) from Dark Souls, it's hard to ignore how many barefoot women are roaming Miyazaki's fictional worlds. Elden Ring's Malenia is rocking bare feet, too, although hers are metal prosthetics. The game's beaches even differentiate between barefoot players and those who are wearing footwear.
So what's with all the shoeless women in Souls games? According to Miyazaki, it's about depicting the human experience. Or something.
"I feel like I’m trying to depict some side of human nature or the human existence that is difficult to describe,” he elaborated.
points: A prolific Japanese game developer has finally addressed all that weird foot imagery in his video games.

videos.summary: Once you leave The Blood of Dawnwalker’s prologue, you’re free to explore the world however you want, and that can be overwhelming. You might not know how to start chipping away at the main quest, and you definitely don’t want to wander into a late-game area and get one-shotted by elite soldiers.
points: Once you leave The Blood of Dawnwalker’s prologue, you’re free to explore the world however you want, and that can be overwhelming.
You might not know how to start chipping away at the main quest, and you definitely don’t want to wander into a late-game area and get one-shotted by elite soldiers.
Fear not: this video guide has 10 things that will give you the best possible start to your journey of revenge.
